findings.finding: Agents who understood others best (top half) survived 74% vs 72% and had 1.08 vs 0.91 children. Comprehension vs children: ρ = 0.09, p = 0.006, n = 959; speaker clarity vs children: ρ = 0.11, p = 0.002, n = 959.
findings.evidence: 959 completed lives with enough tables to measure.

findings.q: How much rests on misunderstanding?
findings.finding: 0% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 8 of 45 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Wrenford "telo" = wood: misheard: thelo → telo (generation 6) · Wrenford "kalo" = two: coined for "tools" by Dace·6 (generation 6) · Oakhollow "telo" = wood: misheard: thelo → telo (generation 6)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.34, p = 0.278, n = 12. Most used: two (6% replaced per generation), wood (12% replaced per generation), food (2% replaced per generation); least: four (36%), five (51%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 17, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.12, p = 0.281, n = 80.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
